## Sample kind

- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
# The Unmapped Floor

There is a claim that gets repeated so often it has the smooth feel of a fact people have stopped questioning: we know the surface of Mars better than we know the bottom of our own oceans. It is roughly true. For decades, spacecraft have photographed and mapped nearly every square kilometer of the Martian surface at resolutions fine enough to pick out boulders and dune ripples. Meanwhile, by most estimates, only about a quarter of the seafloor has been mapped with comparable detail. The rest has been sketched, interpolated, or guessed at from satellite measurements of gravity, which bend subtly around underwater mountains and trenches. We have, in a meaningful sense, looked harder at a dead planet a hundred million miles away than at the floor beneath the boats we sail on.

I find this fact more unsettling than it has any right to be. It isn't that the ocean is a secret. Nobody hid it. It is simply that the ocean is hard in a way that space is not, at least not in the particular ways that matter for mapping. Water absorbs light and radio waves quickly, so you cannot see through it from above with the tools that work so well from orbit. Sound travels well in water, which is why sonar works, but sonar is slow. A ship must trundle back and forth across the sea, pinging the bottom, building a picture one swath at a time. The deep ocean is crushing, dark, and cold, and everything we send down there has to be built to survive it. So the map grows the way a coastline erodes or a stain spreads: patiently, unevenly, one ship's track at a time.

There is something almost moving about the mapping projects that do this work. Among them is an international effort called Seabed 2030, which aims to map the entire ocean floor by the end of the decade. Its goal sounds modest until you consider what it requires. The people involved are not glamorous. They are hydrographers and data processors, many of them working on research vessels for weeks at a stretch, watching screens that show the bottom rising and falling in stripes of color. When they succeed, the result will not look like the photographs of Mars that circulate online, with their crisp craters and their rust-red plains. It will look like a patient accumulation of soundings, an averaged portrait of a place no human will ever see with their own eyes.

---

I have been thinking about maps for a long time, and not in any professional way. I think about them the way some people think about old houses they once lived in, with a kind of tender suspicion. A map is always a promise and always a lie. It promises that the territory has been understood, reduced to lines and labels a stranger can follow. It lies by simplifying, by choosing what to include and what to leave blank. The medieval mapmakers who wrote *here be dragons* on the edges of their charts were, in one sense, being honest. They knew the blank spaces were real. What they got wrong was the idea that the blankness was about monsters rather than about their own ignorance.

Blank spaces on a map do something to the mind. They create a particular tension, a sense that the world is larger than the picture of it we carry around. I suspect this is one reason people are so drawn to the deep sea, to the cave systems still being explored, to the unclimbed peaks in remote ranges. These places are not dangerous in the way a battlefield is dangerous. They are dangerous in the way a question is dangerous. They keep asking whether our sense of the world is complete, and the honest answer is always no.

The seafloor is an especially good example because it is so much a part of ordinary life without being part of ordinary experience. Almost every person alive depends on it indirectly. Undersea cables carry most of the world's internet traffic, threading across the bottom between continents, and they are laid and repaired by ships that must know exactly what terrain they are crossing. Oil and gas platforms sit on it. Fish live on and above it, and the fishing that feeds millions depends on understanding where the ridges and shelves are. Tsunamis begin on it, when tectonic plates slip and push the water above them into motion. A community on a coast might be safer or more endangered depending on how well a submarine slope has been measured. And yet most of us have never once thought about the shape of the bottom of the sea. It is a foundation so deep and so taken for granted that it becomes invisible.

---

I want to be careful not to romanticize ignorance. It is tempting, when faced with blank spaces, to say that mystery is good in itself, that the unmapped is somehow purer than the known. I don't believe that. A seafloor that has been mapped is a seafloor where a tsunami warning can be issued with more confidence, where a cable can be routed around a dangerous trench, where a marine reserve can be drawn to protect a fragile coral garden that would otherwise be dragged up by a trawl. Knowledge in this case is not a luxury. It is a form of care. You cannot protect what you have not seen.

Still, there is a difference between mapping a place and possessing it, and I think the mapping of the deep ocean is interesting precisely because it is not a conquest in the old sense. The seafloor was not discovered in the way that European explorers "discovered" continents that already had people living on them. Its features already had names in the languages of the people who fished and navigated near its shallows. The deep ocean is not really a frontier waiting for flags. It is closer to a very large room whose lights we are slowly switching on, and the room was never empty.

There is a quieter lesson in the way these maps are made, too. Every sounding is an estimate. The instrument sends out a pulse, the pulse bounces back, and the time it takes is converted into a distance using an assumed speed of sound, which varies with temperature, salinity, and pressure. Get any of those wrong and the bottom is in the wrong place. Mapmakers must constantly correct, cross-check, and reconcile. The final chart is therefore not a window onto reality but a carefully constructed argument about reality, supported by evidence and open to revision. I find that honest in a way I wish more of our certainties were.

---

When I say I am interested in maps, I suppose I mean I am interested in the relationship between attention and knowledge. A map records what someone has paid attention to. The blank spaces are not just places nobody has measured; they are places nobody has yet bothered, or been able, to look at closely. This makes me think about how much of my own life is a kind of blank space to my own attention. I know the names of distant mountains I have never seen, the plots of novels I have skimmed, the general shape of economies I do not understand, while the texture of my own street, the particular habits of the people I live with, the sound of my own kitchen in the morning, remain largely uncharted. We are more fluent in the distant than in the near. Perhaps this is a human tendency, the same one that makes us put more effort into studying Mars than into the ocean at the edge of our own cities.

I do not think the answer is to map everything at equal resolution. That is impossible, and it would not even be desirable. A good map is selective. It tells you what matters for the journey you are about to take. A sailor needs the depths near the harbor more than the depths in the middle of the Pacific. A hiker needs the contour lines of the ridge she is climbing and not the coastline of a country she will never visit. But the selectivity should be a choice, made consciously, and the blank spaces should be acknowledged as blank rather than filled with confident fiction.

Maybe that is what the old mapmakers understood, in their awkward way, when they drew sea monsters in the margins. They were admitting that their knowledge had an edge, and that beyond it lay things they could not yet name. The mistake was not the admission. The mistake was assuming that the edge was permanent, that what lay beyond it could never be brought inside.

---

I think often about a particular image from one of the deep-sea expeditions that surveyed the bottom of a trench. The submersible's lights reveal, in a small circle, a landscape of pale sediment and strange animals: tube worms, sea cucumbers, a fish with a face like a startled old man. The creatures have adapted to a world without sunlight, living on chemical energy seeping from vents in the crust. Their existence is a reminder that life is more inventive than our expectations, and that the places we assume to be empty are often full. Every new survey brings up species that nobody had described before. The count of what we do not know keeps growing alongside the count of what we do.

It would be easy to find this discouraging. We will never finish. The ocean is vast, its depths are vaster, and the rate at which we map and catalog it will always be slower than the rate at which our curiosity spawns new questions. But I find it more hopeful than discouraging. A world that can always be explored further is a world that will keep surprising us. It keeps the possibility of wonder open, which is perhaps the most valuable thing a map can preserve.

There is also something humbling in the thought that the most ordinary parts of our planet remain so incompletely known. We live in the age of instant global imagery, of satellites that photograph any address on earth on demand. And yet the floor of the sea, which covers most of the planet's surface and holds most of its water, is still largely a rumor. It reminds me that our sense of having figured things out is often a sense of having looked at the most convenient parts first.

---

So if I had to end with a practical recommendation, it would be this: be suspicious of any map that looks finished. Look for the margins where the lines thin out and the labels become guesses. Ask who measured the thing you are relying on, how long ago, with what instrument, and how much they had to assume. Notice the places where your own picture of the world has been drawn from secondhand sketches rather than firsthand soundings. Most of us carry around enormous, confident maps of subjects we have never personally investigated, and the confidence is often borrowed.

And then, if you can, go and take a few soundings of your own. Read a primary source instead of a summary. Walk a street you have only ever driven down. Ask a question of someone whose life is different from yours and listen to the answer rather than checking it against your existing chart. The deep ocean will keep its secrets for a while yet, and so will most of the people and places around us. There is a kind of quiet joy in finding that the blank spaces are still there, waiting, and that you are free to begin filling in a few of them yourself, one careful line at a time.
---
